items.title: 68002_Benny Waters oral history interview
items.q: And I could fake it and Driver could fake it and the trumpet player could fake, and we had the right harmonies.

ctx.x: No, not at all. But he had a beautiful sound. I'll tell you the effect that he had on this instrument. It was like a violin playin' the melody. To tell you the truth, I think he played a C clarinet, and that case, he could play the violin parts. [ ] I'm sure he was playing a C clarinet. In that case he could play the violin parts, you know. And that's what he was taking the effect of, just the melody, never did - he didn't even make riffs. We were the ones that made it. For instance, he would play a melody on one…

most of the time we faked it, things like that. And the riffs that we were playing is similar to the things that you hearing today. [ ], three-part harmony - alto, trombone and trumpet. So he was just (sings), you know, one of those kind of things. And the, we could do that very fast, we could do it real easy because everybody had big ears, you know, they could hear, see. And I could fake it and Driver could fake it and the trumpet player could fake, and we had the right harmonies.

Some of the first solos, conceived, improvised jazz solos that we recognize as such now, that we can learn about - those of us who weren't there then - through records, seem to indicate to us that the people who were really doin' it, maybe the only ones who were doin' it at first, were Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong on the disc. 'Course it was King Oliver, at least for that matter there was Frankie Trumbauer, Johnny Dodds. When you say they were taking jazz solos as we would recognize them today as jazz solos…
